picks.title: StemDeck is a free, open-source stem separation tool that runs entirely on your machine
picks.excerpt: Solo developer Thales Pereira has released StemDeck, a free open-source stem separation tool for Windows, macOS and Linux that runs entirely locally. He built it to help his kid practice drums, without a subscription or uploading music to someone else's server.
picks.rationale: The most immediately usable item in the pool: subscription-free, offline stem splitting on all three platforms, downloadable today.

picks.title: Universal Music Group partners with Hook to license fan-created remixes across social media
picks.excerpt: UMG has partnered with Hook to license fan-created remixes and mashups across social platforms, turning derivative fan edits into a tracked, payable format instead of takedown fodder.
picks.rationale: Turns the biggest major label's catalogue into legal remix material, moving fan edits from takedown risk to a credited, paid format.

picks.title: I AM CHOIR turns a single sung take into a full choir that follows your lyrics — processed locally
picks.excerpt: AM I AUDIO's I AM CHOIR turns a single sung take into a full choir part that follows your lyrics, melody, phrasing and timing — processed locally, no cloud round-trip. A neural vocal instrument aimed squarely at arrangement work.
picks.rationale: A neural instrument that replaces a session choir from one take, and keeps the vocal on your own machine instead of a cloud service.

picks.title: Cleaning up vocal rips with LALAL.AI's new Lynx separation algorithm
picks.excerpt: A hands-on tutorial on salvaging vocal samples ripped from the internet or vinyl using LALAL.AI's new Lynx separation algorithm, then treating the artefacts so the acapella sits in a track. Craft-level detail on where AI separation still needs a human ear.
picks.rationale: The craft half of the separation story: exactly where Lynx's output still breaks, and the post-treatment that makes a ripped acapella usable.

picks.title: Musicians are asking the wrong question about AI — train a model on your own back catalogue
picks.excerpt: An argument that musicians have been asking the wrong question about AI: instead of fighting models trained on everyone's catalogue, train a private model on your own back catalogue and treat it as a personal collaborator. A practical how-to framing for artist-owned models.
picks.rationale: Reframes the training-data fight into something an individual artist can act on: a private model built only from their own work.
